items.prompt: State what is meant by the term disease.
items.canonical_answer: A disease is a disorder that impairs the normal working of part or all of the body and shows itself through signs and symptoms.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, a disorder that impairs the normal working of the body. This definition is a statement of what disease means; naming one disease, or saying that a person feels ill, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Sickle cell anaemia is inherited, and TB is caused by bacteria. State one difference between a non-infectious disease such as sickle cell anaemia and an infectious disease such as TB.
items.canonical_answer: A non-infectious disease such as sickle cell anaemia is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed from person to person, whereas an infectious disease such as TB is caused by a pathogen and can be passed on.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for one clear difference: whether a pathogen causes it, or whether it can be passed from person to person. The answer must contrast the two diseases, for example with whereas; describing one of them alone earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term pathogen.
items.canonical_answer: A pathogen is an organism or virus that causes disease.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, an organism or virus that causes disease. The definition must include viruses as well as organisms; a statement that a pathogen is a germ or a bacterium is too narrow.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Measles is caused by a Morbillivirus. State one feature of a virus that shows it is not a bacterium.
items.canonical_answer: A virus is not a cell: it consists of nucleic acid in a protein coat. It also reproduces inside the cells of a host and nowhere else.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for one feature: not made of cells (no cytoplasm or nucleus, just nucleic acid in a protein coat), or reproduces inside host cells.
A feature of bacteria, such as having a cell wall, does not answer the question. Antibiotics acting on bacteria but not viruses is a consequence, not a feature.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term vector, as in the vector of malaria.
items.canonical_answer: A vector is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another. The vector of malaria is the female Anopheles mosquito.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another. The statement of the term must say the vector is an organism; naming the female Anopheles mosquito is an example, not the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: After floods in a settlement near Katima Mulilo that has no toilets, many people develop cholera. Explain how the cholera bacterium passes from an infected person to a new host.
items.canonical_answer: The faeces of an infected person contain Vibrio cholerae. Because there are no toilets, the faeces and the bacteria reach the river or well that people use, so the water becomes contaminated. Another person then swallows the bacteria in the water or in food washed in it, which leads to infection of the intestine.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: how the bacteria leave one person and reach the water, in the faeces entering a water supply (1); how the new host takes them in, by swallowing contaminated water or food (1).
The route is faeces to mouth. An answer that gives a mosquito, droplets in the air or touching an infected person as the route earns no mark, because cholera is water-borne and has no vector.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A learner says that malaria passes from a sick person to a healthy one when the sick person coughs, or when they share drinking water. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to treat malaria as an airborne or water-borne disease. In fact malaria needs a vector, the female Anopheles mosquito: she picks up the parasite from an infected person's blood, the parasite must develop in her, and she passes it on in a later bite. The test is to ask what the vector is and what must happen inside it. Coughing and water have no such step.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that malaria is passed by droplets or water instead of by a vector (1); the correct idea, that the female Anopheles mosquito carries it and the parasite must develop in her before she can infect another person, or the test (1).
The card is a discrimination between vector-borne and other routes, not a repeat of the definition of malaria. A confusion with cholera, which is water-borne, is the likely source of the mistake.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by sanitation, as used in the control of cholera.
items.canonical_answer: Sanitation means the safe disposal of human waste so that faeces do not contaminate water or food.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, the safe disposal of human waste (faeces or sewage). The definition must be about waste; saying that sanitation is making water safe to drink is confused with water treatment and earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Families in a village in Kavango are given insecticide-treated bed nets. Explain how the nets reduce the spread of malaria.
items.canonical_answer: The net is a barrier between the sleeping person and the female Anopheles mosquito, which tends to bite at night, so fewer bites occur. The insecticide kills or repels mosquitoes that land on it, which reduces the number of mosquitoes that live long enough to pick up the parasite and pass it on, so fewer people are infected.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the net blocks bites, so there is less chance of the parasite entering a person (1); the insecticide kills or repels mosquitoes, which results in fewer infected mosquitoes passing the parasite to others (1).
The mechanism must target the mosquito. An answer about the net killing the parasite inside a person, or purifying water, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A man in Oshakati is treated for TB with several antibiotics for six months. After two months he feels well and stops taking the tablets. Explain why this is a problem, using the information given.
items.canonical_answer: In this case the bacteria grow slowly, so some of them survive after he feels better. Because he stopped early, the survivors multiply and the disease returns, and he can pass it on to others. Some survivors may resist the antibiotics, so the TB may become harder to treat.
marking_guidance: 2 marks, each tied to the given situation: some bacteria survive although he feels well, so they multiply and the disease returns or can spread (1); the survivors may be resistant, so the disease becomes harder to treat (1).
The information given is that he stopped after two months of a six-month course. An answer that says he should follow the doctor's advice, with no biological reason, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A community plans to control malaria by chlorinating its well water and building pit latrines. Explain the error in this plan.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to propose measures aimed at cholera instead of malaria. In fact malaria is controlled by targeting the mosquito and the parasite: draining standing water, using treated nets and spraying, and treating infected people with antimalarial drugs. Chlorination and latrines break the route of faeces to mouth, which does not carry malaria. The test is whether the measure breaks the mosquito's breeding or biting, or the parasite's spread in people.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the measures do not target the mosquito or the parasite (1); the correct idea, that control uses nets, removal of standing water, insecticides or drugs, or the test (1).

The card is a discrimination between the control of a vector-borne and a water-borne disease. Water treatment and latrines are sound for cholera and are not harmful in themselves, so do not credit an answer that says they are.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term endemic, as in malaria is endemic in parts of northern Namibia.
items.canonical_answer: A disease is endemic in a region when it is present there at a steady level over many years.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, present in a region at a steady level over many years. The term describes constant presence; a sudden rise in cases is an outbreak, which is not the same thing.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 2.8.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Malaria is common in warm, wet lowlands near the Okavango and rare in cold highland regions. Explain how climate causes this pattern.
items.canonical_answer: Warm, wet conditions let Anopheles breed, because the female lays eggs in standing water left by rain. The parasite also needs enough warmth to develop in the mosquito, so in cold highlands it cannot complete development, which leads to few infections. Malaria is therefore common where both conditions are met.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: rain gives standing water for the mosquito to breed in, so there are more mosquitoes (1); the parasite needs high enough temperature to develop in the mosquito, which results in little malaria where it is cold (1).
Treat these as tendencies: the temperature needed differs between parasite species, so a single value is not required.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which type of organism causes cholera?
A  a virus
B  a bacterium
C  a protoctist
D  a fungus

2. Which row matches a disease with the type of pathogen that causes it?
A  malaria: a bacterium
B  TB: a virus
C  HIV/AIDS: a virus
D  measles: a protoctist

3. A pathogen has no cytoplasm and reproduces inside living host cells. Which pathogen is it?
A  Vibrio cholerae
B  Plasmodium vivax
C  Mycobacterium tuberculosis
D  the human immunodeficiency virus

4. What is the vector of malaria?
A  the female Anopheles mosquito
B  contaminated drinking water
C  the male Anopheles mosquito
D  droplets from a cough

5. A boy drinks from a river below a village with no toilets and develops severe watery diarrhoea. How was the pathogen most likely passed on?
A  in droplets from a cough
B  by a mosquito bite
C  in water contaminated with faeces
D  by contact with infected blood

6. How is TB of the lungs usually passed from one person to another?
A  by breathing in droplets released when an infected person coughs
B  by a mosquito that fed on an infected person
C  by drinking water that contains faeces
D  by sharing a cup with an infected person

7. Which action carries a risk of passing on HIV?
A  hugging an infected friend
B  sharing a drinking cup
C  being bitten by a mosquito
D  using an injection needle that was used by an infected person

8. Which measure targets the breeding of the mosquito that carries malaria?
A  treating drinking water with chlorine
B  draining pools of standing water near homes
C  building pit latrines
D  covering the mouth when coughing

9. Several unvaccinated children in a village have measles. Which action does most to prevent spread to other children?
A  spraying the walls of homes with insecticide
B  treating the village well with chlorine
C  vaccinating the children who are not yet immune
D  draining pools of standing water

10. A patient with TB stops taking antibiotics after two months because she feels well. What is the main biological risk?
A  The surviving bacteria can multiply and may become resistant.
B  The antibiotics begin to damage her lung cells.
C  She becomes a vector of the disease.
D  She becomes permanently immune to TB.

11. Which conditions best favour the spread of malaria?
A  cold, dry highlands
B  cold, wet highlands
C  warm, dry desert
D  warm, wet lowland with standing water

12. A region has 900 mm of rain a year but is at high altitude, with a mean temperature of about 12 degrees Celsius, and malaria is rare there. Which is the best explanation?
A  Heavy rain washes the parasite away.
B  The temperature is too low for the parasite to develop in the mosquito.
C  Anopheles lays eggs in cold water but not in warm water.
D  The parasite is spread by water, which is scarce.
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 D, 4 A, 5 C, 6 A, 7 D, 8 B, 9 C, 10 A, 11 D, 12 B.
1. Vibrio cholerae is a bacterium (B). A is the error of giving the cause of measles or HIV; C is the cause of malaria; D has no basis in this topic.
2. HIV is a virus (C). A gives malaria the wrong type, since a protoctist causes it; B reverses TB, which bacteria cause; D gives measles the type of malaria, but a virus causes measles.
3. A virus is not a cell and reproduces in host cells (D). A and C are bacteria, which are cells with cytoplasm; B is a protoctist, which is also a cell.
4. The female Anopheles mosquito carries the parasite (A). B is the cholera route, the error of mixing a water-borne with a vector-borne disease; C is wrong because the female takes the blood meals; D is the TB route.
5. Cholera is passed from faeces to mouth through contaminated water (C). A is the TB route; B is the malaria route; D is a route for HIV.
6. Droplets from a cough carry the bacteria into the lungs of another person (A). B is the malaria error; C is the cholera error; D is a casual-contact error, since sharing a cup is not the usual route for TB or HIV.
7. Blood-to-blood contact through a shared needle can pass on HIV (D). A and B are casual contact, which does not pass on the virus; C is the error of treating HIV as vector-borne, like malaria.
8. Anopheles lays eggs in standing water, so draining it reduces mosquitoes (B). A and C are cholera measures, the error in the misconception register; D is a measure for an airborne disease such as TB.
9. Vaccination makes children immune before they meet the virus (C). A and D are malaria measures that do not stop a virus spread in droplets; B is a cholera measure.
10. Surviving bacteria multiply and some may resist the antibiotics (A). B invents a harm that is not the reason; C misuses vector, since a person with TB passes it on directly in droplets; D is wrong because stopping the course does not give immunity.
11. Warmth lets the parasite develop in the mosquito and standing water lets Anopheles breed (D). A and B fail on temperature; C fails on water.
12. Low temperature stops the parasite from developing in the mosquito (B). A has no basis; C reverses the mosquito's needs; D is the water-borne error, since malaria needs a vector.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test application to a described situation.

Each distractor is a named error: the route of one disease given to another (cholera, malaria and TB mixed up), a vector credited to a water-borne disease, a malaria measure offered for cholera, casual contact treated as a route for HIV.

items.prompt:
A health team in northern Namibia recorded the following in four districts. These figures are our own invented values.

| District | Mean annual rainfall (mm) | Mean temperature (°C) | Malaria cases per 1000 people in one year |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 600 | 24 | 85 |
| B | 450 | 23 | 40 |
| C | 250 | 22 | 6 |
| D | 120 | 20 | 1 |

(a) State the type of pathogen that causes malaria, and name the vector. [2]
(b) Describe the pattern shown in the table. [2]
(c) Explain how rainfall could cause this pattern. [2]
(d) Suggest one way that the health team could reduce the number of cases in district A, with a reason. [1]
(e) Suggest one social or economic reason why cases in district A may stay high even when a control measure is available. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A protoctist (a Plasmodium parasite); the female Anopheles mosquito.
(b) The number of cases per 1000 people decreases as rainfall decreases: 85 in district A, with 600 mm, falls to 1 in district D, with 120 mm. Temperature also decreases from 24 °C to 20 °C across the same districts.
(c) More rain leaves more pools of standing water, which lets more Anopheles lay eggs and breed, so there are more mosquitoes and more bites, and more people are infected.
(d) Supply insecticide-treated nets, because they block bites and kill mosquitoes; or drain standing pools, because this removes breeding sites.
(e) Families may not be able to afford nets or may not use them; or a clinic is too far or too costly to visit, so people go untreated.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for protoctist, 1 mark for the female Anopheles mosquito (the vector); (b) 2 marks from three points: cases decrease as rainfall decreases, a figure quoted from the table, the highest in A and the lowest in D; (c) 2 marks from three points: rain makes standing water, so more breeding sites, so more mosquitoes or more bites.

(d) 1 mark for a measure that targets the mosquito or the parasite (nets, draining water, insecticide, antimalarial drugs) with its reason; chlorinating water is not credited. (e) 1 mark for a social or economic reason, for example cost or distance to a clinic. Parts (a) and (b) credit AO A (4 marks); parts (c) to (e) credit AO B (4 marks). Answers must use the table, not a general statement; a term such as vector must be used correctly.
